title: Beef Wellington
subtitle: Beef fillet wrapped in mushroom duxelles and puff pastry
excerpt: A whole beef fillet coated in a layer of mushroom duxelles and Parma ham, wrapped in puff pastry and baked until the pastry is golden and the beef inside is perfectly medium-rare. A showstopper roast for celebrations.

recipe.sourceNotes: Beef Wellington is most often attributed to the British tradition, though similar dishes of meat wrapped in pastry appear in French and German cooking (filet de boeuf en croûte, Rinderfilet im Teigmantel). The dish was popularised in Britain during the 1960s and 1970s and became a classic of the dinner-party repertoire. The name is commonly linked to the Duke of Wellington, the hero of Waterloo, though documentary evidence for this connection is thin. The critical challenge of the dish is keeping the pastry base from becoming soggy: the duxelles must be cooked completely dry, and the beef must be seared and chilled before wrapping.

recipeTools.notes: Essential for getting the beef to exactly the right internal temperature.

content.text: Two things prevent a soggy bottom: dry duxelles and cold beef. Cook the mushrooms until every trace of moisture is gone. They should look almost paste-like and the pan should be completely dry. Sear the beef, then chill it for at least 30 minutes in the fridge before wrapping. The cold beef prevents the pastry from starting to cook before the oven does. Do not skip either step. For medium-rare, the internal temperature should be 52 to 54 C when it comes out of the oven: it will rise another 3 to 4 C during the rest.

Make the duxelles: melt the butter in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms, garlic, and thyme. Cook, stirring often, for 15 to 20 minutes until completely dry and paste-like. Season. Spread onto a tray to cool completely.

Season the beef generously. Heat the oil in a frying pan over the highest heat. Sear the fillet for 1 to 2 minutes on all sides until well browned all over. Brush all surfaces with Dijon mustard while still hot. Cool for 20 minutes, then chill in the fridge for at least 30 minutes.

Lay a large sheet of cling film on the work surface. Overlap the Parma ham slices to form a rectangle large enough to wrap the beef. Spread the cold duxelles evenly over the ham. Place the beef at one end and roll tightly in the cling film, twisting the ends to form a tight cylinder. Chill for at least 20 minutes.

Heat the oven to 220 C / fan 200 C / gas 7. Roll out the puff pastry on a lightly floured surface. Unwrap the beef roll and place it on the pastry. Wrap the pastry around it, trim the excess, and seal the edges with beaten egg. Place seam-side down on a lined baking tray. Brush all surfaces with egg wash. Score the surface lightly with a sharp knife. Chill for 15 minutes.

Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastry is deep golden. The internal temperature should read 52 to 54 C for medium-rare. Rest uncovered for 10 minutes. Slice with a sharp, serrated knife and serve immediately.
